responses_archetypeVariants.sophisticate: The sophisticate does not say cheer up. He treats aggregate life-satisfaction data as evidence — a real empirical claim that most lives are net-positive, and therefore that the wager pays out for nearly everyone. That is the version worth answering, and it fails at the inference rather than the data. Concede the surveys exist and are stable across cultures. Self-report still cannot bridge to objective welfare, because the instrument doing the rating is the same nervous system whose output is being rated, and selection has no stake in calibrating that instrument for accuracy — only for persistence. The one systematic, well-documented mood-linked distortion of self-appraisal runs upward. Optimism bias and the positive-illusions program (Taylor and Brown) find that mildly inflated self-assessment is the signature of psychological health and that more accurate appraisal tracks depression; the field defends these illusions on adaptiveness, never on accuracy. Grant that and the cheerful baseline is the documented distortion wearing the costume of normalcy, and the defeater disqualifies the optimist's read first and hardest. Three truncations compound it: adaptation flattens reported satisfaction across wildly different objective conditions, so the paraplegic and the lottery winner converge within two years — which indicts the instrument, not the conditions; social-desirability pressure inflates the upward read, since admitting a bad life invites pathologization; and survivorship silently deletes the worst outcomes — the suicides, the unrescuable, the dead infants file no response. But grant even all of this is wrong. Grant the surveys pristine and ninety percent of lives genuinely net-positive. The argument is untouched, because it was never an averages argument. Procreation is a non-consensual wager run on a third party, and the ten percent who draw catastrophically never agreed to play for the comfort of the winners. You do not get to gamble with someone else's welfare and then exhibit the people who happened to win as the justification for the people who lost.
